4.26.m:
Śaunaka said:
I wish to hear from you, O wise one; explain from the very root
the merit in keeping an oath and what sin there is in breaking it.

Or what happens in a false oath and in a true one, O sage,
having given the right hand? Show mercy, O ocean of mercy!

Sūta said:
Listen, O tiger among sages; I shall explain from the very root.
You are foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the welfare of all people.

The fruit a man obtains by giving a hundred cows—
ten million times greater than that is the merit in keeping an oath, O twice-born.

From breaking an oath, a fool goes to a terrible hell;
he is roasted for a hundred Manvantaras, there is no doubt of this.

Then, having obtained a birth here in the house of a pauper,
he is destitute of food and clothing, and suffers through his own actions.

If one takes an oath falsely in the presence of the gods, fire, and the guru,
so long does his body burn, [yet] Viṣṇu's lineage is not destroyed.

Regarding a false oath, O brahmin, what can I say now?
For a hundred Manvantaras, O brahmin, [he goes to] hell; what more of falsehood?

Having touched the floral offerings of Śrī Hari falsely, O best of sages,
he takes seven ancestors and is roasted in hell for a long time.

Sometime obtaining a birth, he becomes a leper in birth after birth.
If it is so even with truth, O brahmin, what is to be said of falsehood?

The mortal who, having given his right hand, keeps it—
his attainment becomes Kṛṣṇa; I speak the truth, truly.

Having given his hand, the mortal who does not keep his word,
so long do his ancestors experience torments.

He himself, O tiger among sages, goes to an exceedingly dreadful hell,
and dead, he goes with ten million ancestors [to suffer]; there is no doubt.

Śaunaka said:
Who of old attained Kṛṣṇa from keeping [the pledge of] his hand,
of the right hand, O sage? Tell me, I wish to hear with respect.

Sūta said:
Of old, in a certain city, there was a Śūdra named Vīravikrama,
who ate much, had a stout body, was talkative, and very handsome.
He was wealthy, endowed with sons, cultured, learned, dear to all people, / and ever a worshiper of brahmins and guests.
Devoted to his father, O best of the twice-born, he always kept his promises, / obeyed the words of his elders, and served Hari.
Once, an outcaste, handsome, young, and clever, / having assumed the form of a brahmin, came in disguise to his house.
The brahmin said: / Listen to my words, O wise one: my auspicious wife has died. / What shall I do? Where shall I go? Tell me today out of compassion.
If a person arranges a marriage, especially for a brahmin, / what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred bathing places, or for sacrifices and millions of vows?
Having heard this, that Vīravikrama said to the brāhmaṇa: / "Hear my word, O brāhmaṇa: my maiden daughter is [yet] a child."
If it is your desire, O brahmin, I will give her [to you] according to the rites; / I give my right hand, and it will not be otherwise.
Hearing this word of his, the outcaste seized his right hand. / Filled with joy, he indeed spoke these words:
The brahmin said: / Having fixed an auspicious moment, give me your auspicious daughter; / in delay there are many obstacles—so it is settled in the scriptures.
Vīravikrama said: / Tomorrow, O brahmin, I will give you my daughter; it cannot be otherwise. / Even a base man, having given his right hand, would not do [the opposite].
Sūta said: / Calling the brahmin Kṛṣṇaśarman, the family priest, / he told him all this, O sage, and related the agreement, O twice-born.
'Why do you wish to give your daughter, being a śūdra, to a brahmin? / Especially do not give her to one who is unknown and of noble lineage.'
All his kinsmen, his father and the rest, said, O one rich in asceticism: / 'Hear our words, dear Vīravikrama:
To one whose family, country, lineage, wealth, / character, and age are not known, a daughter is never given by relatives.'
He said, O best of the twice-born: 'My right hand has been given; / I can by no means ever act otherwise.'
Having spoken thus to them, he proceeded to give the maiden to the brāhmaṇa; / seeing this, all the relatives were filled with wonderful astonishment.
Hearing that truthful word, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace / suddenly appeared, having mounted Garuḍa, O sage.
The blessed Lord said: / Blessed is your family and your virtue, blessed are your mother and father, / blessed is your truthful word, and blessed is your right hand!
Blessed is your deed and your birth; none such exists in the three worlds. / By such a deed, O virtuous one, you deliver your lineage!
Sūta said: / While Śrī Kṛṣṇa was speaking thus, a celestial chariot made of gold arrived, / accompanied by Hari's attendants, bearing Garuḍa's emblem everywhere.
All his family, O brahmin, along with the outcaste and the family priest, / the holder of the conch and lotus placed upon the chariot Himself.
Taking them all, Hari went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha; / there they remained for a long time, enjoying pleasures very hard to attain.
Whoever transgresses his word, or whoever violates his right hand, / goes to hell along with his family; truly, truly do I say this.
His food and water, O brahmin, cannot be accepted by the ancestors or the gods; / virtue, abandoning his house, flees in terror, O best of the twice-born.
Whatever foolish-minded person, having given hope, causes despair, / goes to hell, dragging along ten million generations of his own people.
Whoever transgresses his word, his virtue is transgressed / by kings, fire, and thieves, O brahmin; truly, truly this is certain.
Having properly heard this Svargottara, one goes beyond heaven; / liberated while living here, he goes hereafter to the supreme abode named after Kṛṣṇa.

5.0.s:
atha śrīpādme mahāpurāṇe pañcamaṃ pātālakhaṇḍaṃ prārabhyate
śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥśrīkuladevatāyai namaḥ
śrīgurucaraṇāraviṃdābhyāṃ namaḥ
5.0.d:
अथ श्रीपाद्मे महापुराणे पञ्चमं पातालखण्डं प्रारभ्यते
श्रीगणेशाय नमःश्रीकुलदेवतायै नमः
श्रीगुरुचरणारविंदाभ्यां नमः
5.0.m:
Now begins the fifth [section], the Pātālakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.

Obeisance to glorious Gaṇeśa! Obeisance to the glorious family deity! / Obeisance to the lotus feet of the glorious guru!

5.1.m:
Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
and to the goddess Sarasvatī and to Vyāsa, one should then recite 'Victory!'

The sages said:
Everything has been heard from you, O fortunate one—the charming Svargakhaṇḍa.
Now, O long-lived one, tell us indeed the deeds of Śrī Rāma.

Sūta said:
Then, on one occasion, the excellent sage Vātsyāyana asked the Lord of Serpents,
the supporter of the earth, this purest account.

the distinct determination of principles such as the creation of the Mahat-principle;
and the diverse deeds of kings have been related by you, O sinless one,

and the wondrous deeds of kings born in the solar dynasty.
Among them is the narrative enacted by Rāma, which removes many great sins.

The story of the horse sacrifice of that heroic Rāma was heard
in brief by me from you; I desire it in full detail—

that which, heard, remembered, and recited, takes away great sins,
grants desired aims, and bestows satisfaction to the minds of devotees.
Śeṣa said: / "Fortunate are you, O best of the twice-born, whose intellect is such, / longing for the nectar of the pair of feet of the hero of Raghu's race.

All sages say that the company of virtuous people is excellent,
from which arises the tale of the lord of the Raghu lineage, destroying sins.

A favor was bestowed upon me by you, in that Rāma was brought to mind again—
he whose feet are illuminated by the jewels from the hosts of diadems of gods and asuras.

In the ocean of the tale of Rāvaṇa's enemy, what is a gnat such as I,
wherein gods such as Brahmā are deluded and do not comprehend?

Nevertheless, O sage, it must be spoken by me to you according to my own capacity;
birds go in the vast sky, relying on their own movement.

The life of the lord of the Raghus extends to a hundred crore [verses];
people speak of it according to the nature of their intellect.

The virtuous renown of the lord of the Raghus will purify my soiled mind
through its own contact, just as fire does to gold.

Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to that excellent sage, with eyes motionless in meditation,
he beheld through knowledge the sublime, auspicious tale.
With a voice choked with emotion and his limbs marked by great joy, / he again narrated the lucid story of Daśaratha's son.
Śeṣa said: / When the lord of Laṅkā, the tormentor of gods and demons, / who stole the beauty of the moon of the lotus faces of the Apsaras troop, was slain,
all the gods, headed by Indra, then attained happiness; / having attained happiness, they offered praise, bowing down like servants.
And having installed the righteous Bibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā, / Rāma, together with Sītā, mounted the Puṣpaka [aerial chariot].
Accompanied then by Sugrīva, Hanumat, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa, / Bibhīṣaṇa too, along with his ministers, followed, eager at the separation.
Beholding Laṅkā in many ways with broken ramparts and city gates, / and seeing the Aśoka grove there, the dwelling place of Sītā, he fainted.
And [seeing] the śiṃśapā trees there, blossoming and full of buds, / strewn with female rākṣasas who had died out of fear of Hanumat,
having quickly seen all this, Rāma set out toward his city, / accompanied by Brahmā and the other gods, each in their own aerial chariots,
hearing the sounds of celestial kettledrums that brought pleasure to the ears, / and being worshipped likewise by the dances of the Apsarases, the best of the Raghus,
showing Sītā on the way the sacred bathing places and hermitage sites, / the sages, the sons of the sages, and the devoted wives of the sages.
Wherever dwellings were previously made by the wise Rāma, / he, together with Lakṣmaṇa, showed them all to her.
Showing it thus to her, Rāma saw his own city; / then, near it, he beheld Nandigrāma.
where King Bharata truly dwelt, protecting dharma, / bearing many signs of grief born of separation from his brother,
sleeping in a ditch, living as a celibate student, wearing matted hair and bark garments, / his slender staff-like body distressed by grief, constantly narrating Rāma's story,
not even eating barley grain, not drinking water frequently, / and who, having bowed to the rising sun, said:
“O eye of the universe, O lord of the gods, remove my great sin! / For my sake, even Rāmacandra, worshipped by the world, went to the forest.
Attended by Sītā of delicate limbs, he went to the wilderness— / that Sītā who felt distress upon a bed of flowers just by encountering a stalk!
That faithful Sītā who never felt the burning heat of the sun, / that Jānakī wanders from forest to forest for my sake! Alas!
That Sītā who was never seen by the eyes of hosts of kings, / that Sītā is now surely seen by Kirātas of death-like form!
That Sītā who, fed with sweet food, did not wish to eat, / that Sītā today desires forest fruits! Alas!”
Approaching the sun thus every day, / the great king Bharata, beloved of Rāma, says this every morning."
And when spoken to by the wise ministers who shared his joy and sorrow, / who knew statecraft and were skilled in the treatises, the king spoke to them:
“O ministers, why do you address me, unfortunate and the lowest of men? / For my sake my elder brother Rāma languishes having reached the forest.
I respectfully perform the cleansing of the sin of my unfortunate mother / by constantly remembering the feet of Rāmacandra, O good ministers!
Blessed exceedingly is Sumitrā, the mother of a hero, dear to her husband, / whose son serves Rāma's feet every day.”
In whichever village Bharata, affectionate toward his brother, indeed stayed / and uttered loud lamentations, that village he saw.

5.2.m: Śeṣa said: / Then, with his mind overwhelmed by longing to see him, / the brother Bharata, foremost of the righteous, was remembered again and again.
And he spoke to the mighty Hanumat, the son of the wind, / his inner darkness destroyed by the splendor of the moon in the guise of his flashing teeth:
“O hero Hanumat, hear my words prompted by [love for] my brother, / faltering and overwhelmed by long separation!
Go, O heroic son of the wind, to that brother / who stubbornly bears a body with a staff-like frame emaciated by separation from me,
who wears bark garments, wears matted hair on his head, / and would not even eat fruits, tormented by separation;
to whom another’s wife is like a mother, and gold is like a clod of earth, / who looks upon the subjects as sons—my kinsman who knows dharma.
Quickly sprinkle him, whose body is burned by the flames of the fire of sorrow born of separation from me, / with a rain of water in the form of news of my arrival!
Announce from joy that Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, / by monkey lords headed by Sugrīva, and by rākṣasas with Bibhīṣaṇa,
has arrived, seated in the Puṣpaka [chariot], / so that this younger brother of mine may quickly attain joy from my arrival.”
Having heard these words of the wise hero of Raghu's line, / the messenger went to Bharata's dwelling named Nandi.
Having gone to Nandigrāma, the wise one saw Bharata, / surrounded well by aged ministers and melting with grief from separation from his brother,
narrating the tale of Rāmacandra to the aged ministers, / brimming over with the nectar of his lotus feet.
He bowed to Bharata, who was dharma incarnate, / fashioned as it were by the Creator with a full portion of goodness alone.
Seeing him, Bharata quickly stood up with folded hands / and said, “Welcome! Tell me of Rāma’s welfare!”
Even as he was speaking thus, his right arm throbbed; / grief departed from his heart, and his face was filled with tears of joy.
Beholding the king like that, the lord of monkeys replied: / “Know that Rāma with Lakṣmaṇa has arrived near the city!”
His body sprinkled with the nectar of the message of Rāma's arrival, / he attained a flood of joy; I, the thousand-faced one, do not know [its extent]!
He said: “There is nothing of mine that could be given to you by me; / I am your servant for the rest of my life, O bringer of Rāma's message!”
Vasiṣṭha also took the water offering; and the aged ministers, overjoyed, / went toward Rāmacandra along the path shown by Hanumat.
Seeing from afar the delightful Rāmacandra approaching, / seated in the Puṣpaka [chariot], with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
and Rāma also seeing Bharata coming on foot, / wearing matted hair, bark garments, and a loincloth,
he saw the ministers dressed like his brother, identically clad, wearing matted hair, / their forms emaciated by constant weariness from austerities.
Rāma also thought, upon seeing the king like that: / “Ah! This son of Daśaratha, the wise king of kings,
comes on foot, wearing the dress of matted hair and bark garments! / Truly, no other sorrow of mine while dwelling in the forest
was like that which turns about in his mind through separation from me! / Ah, look at my brother, my friend dearer than life!
Hearing that I have arrived nearby, with overjoyed aged ministers / and accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, Bharata comes to see me.”
Speaking thus, the lord of men [descended] from the Puṣpaka [chariot] into the courtyard of the sky, / shown honor by Bibhīṣaṇa, Hanūmat, and Lakṣmaṇa.
He descended swiftly from the vehicle, his heart melted with longing, / crying out again and again, "O brother, brother, and again brother, brother, brother!"
Seeing that Rāmacandra had disembarked accompanied by the gods, / the wise Bharata, melted with longing for his brother, beheld him; / and shedding tears of joy, he bowed down prostrate like a staff.
Raghunātha too, seeing him fallen prostrate like a staff upon the earth, / raised him up and embraced him with both arms, his gaze filled with joy.
Though raised up, he did not stand up at all, weeping repeatedly, / his arms clinging firmly in grasp around Rāmacandra's lotus feet.
Bharata said: / "Have mercy on me, wicked, vicious, and sinful as I am, / O Rāmacandra, mighty-armed one, out of compassion, O treasure of mercy!
That very foot which deemed the touch of the Videha princess's hand too harsh, / wandered in the forest, O Rāma, on my account!"
Having spoken thus, distressed, his face covered in tears, embracing [him] again and again, / he stood before [him] with joined palms, his face overcome with joy.
Raghunātha, the ocean of compassion, having embraced his younger brother, / bowing and respectfully inquiring after the chief counselor,
sat upon the seat of the Puṣpaka together with his brother Bharata. / Bharata beheld Sītā, his blameless sister-in-law.
Was she Anasūyā to Atri, or Lopāmudrā to the pot-born [Agastya]? / He regarded the devoted wife, the daughter of Janaka, and bowed down to her.
"Mother, forgive whatever sin was committed by me, devoid of sense. / Women devoted to their husbands like you bring welfare to all."
The illustrious daughter of Janaka too, looking upon her brother-in-law with affection, / bestowed blessings upon him and inquired about his well-being.
All those who had mounted that excellent aerial chariot in the courtyard of the sky / beheld within a moment their father's city close at hand.

5.3.m: Śeṣa said: / Having seen the capital city, the dwelling place of his own people, / the wise and heroic Rāma, eager to see it after a long time, rejoiced.
Bharata too sent his friend, the minister named Sumukha, / toward the city to arrange for the city festival.
Bharata said: / "Let the people quickly prepare the festival of Raghunātha's arrival, / delightful in every mansion, with various festive arrangements.
Let the royal highways be cleared of dust, sprinkled with sandalwood water, / decorated with masses of flowers, and crowded with glad and flourishing people.
Let all their courtyards be decorated with the luster of colorful banners; / let the monkeys look upon it just like a rainbow at the arrival of clouds.
Let people cause incense of aloe to be burnt in every home, / seeing whose smoke the peacocks may dance at play.
Let them decorate my mountain-like elephants, well-governed by drivers, / in many ways with red chalk and other secondary minerals.
Let swift horses, painted beautifully, shine repeatedly, / at the mere sight of whose speed the steed of heaven abandons its pride.
Let thousands of lovely maidens adorned with all ornaments, / mounted upon elephants, scatter pearls.
Let the wives of brāhmaṇas, holding vessels with dūrvā grass and turmeric, / auspicious married women, perform the lustration of the great king Rāma.
May Kausalyā, distressed at the message of reunion with her son, / though very emaciated, attain joy, greatly eager to behold him."
"Let the joyful populace make such arrangements / that bring beauty to the city for the arrival of Rāma."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech, Sumukha, best of counselors, / went to the city to erect festive archways.
Having reached that city, the minister named Sumukha / announced to the people the great festival of Rāma's arrival.
Hearing that Raghunātha had reached the city, the people were exceedingly delighted, / having previously abandoned pleasures and comforts due to separation from him.
Brāhmaṇas accomplished in the Vedas, pure, with darbha grass in their hands / and wrapped in washed upper garments, went to the venerable Raghunāyaka.
Kṣatriyas who were the most heroic, best bearers of bows and arrows, / heroes victorious in battle many times, also went to him.
Vaiśyas abundant in wealth, their hands adorned with coins, / wearing clean white garments, approached the lord of men.
Śūdras who were devoted to twice-borns, steadfast in their own proper conduct, / devoted to Vedic customs, also went to the lord of the city.
Whatever people practiced a trade, established in their own respective work, / taking their own wares, went to the glorious king Rāma.
Thus, at the prince's command, filled with an inundation of joy / and accompanied by various celebrations, they came to the lord of men.
Śeṣa said: / Raghunātha too, surrounded by all the deities in their respective vehicles, / entered high into the city, which had been made enchanting.
The monkeys, leaping about, traversing the pathways of the sky, / their limbs arrayed in their own splendor, followed toward the excellent city.
Having quickly descended from the Puṣpaka, Rāma, together with Sītā / and surrounded by his retinue, then mounted a palanquin.
He then entered Ayodhyā, where festive archways had been erected, / which was crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, and adorned with celebrations.
Shining amid loudly sounded lutes, paṇava drums, bherī drums, and other instruments, / praised by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards:
"Victory to Rāghava Rāma! Victory to the ornament of the solar race! / Victory to the son of Daśaratha, the Lord! May the protector of the worlds be victorious!"
Hearing such auspicious speech of the citizens, whose limbs were thrilled with joy, / who shone with the bristling of their hair born from the sight of Rāma,
he entered the excellent highway, adorned with crossways and squares, / sprinkled with sandalwood water, and furnished with flowers and fresh shoots.
Then certain women of the city, resorting to the openings of the latticed windows, / filled with longing to behold the form of Raghunātha, said:
The women of the city said: / "Blessed indeed were the Bhilla maidens in the forests who drank in Rāma's lotus face / with their blue-lotus eyes—these women whose great fortune came to fruition!
Behold the blessed, lotus-eyed face of Lord Śrī Rāma, the abode of heroism, / the sight of which even the gods headed by Brahmā attained; ah, we too are endowed with great fortune!
Behold this face of sweet smile, its noble head shining with a diadem, / bearing high nostrils and lips whose radiant hue puts the bandhūka flower to shame!"

Looking with glances like lotus petals upon those women who had spoken thus with an abundance of affection, / the teacher of all, joyful, his limbs worn from traveling, desired to go to his mother's house, observing the people who bore an undiminished weight of love.

5.4.m: Vātsyāyana said: / "O sovereign lord of serpents, master capable of bearing the burden of the earth, / listen to a single doubt of mine, and kindly explain it to me.
From the very moment when Raghunātha's departure to the forest took place, / she remained with a void mind within her body,
distressed by separation from him, emaciated in body, and extremely sorrowful; / having heard from the minister Sumukha that Raghunātha had returned,"
How did she rejoice? What happened? What kind of sign was marked there? / What did she say to the one who brought the message of Rāmacandra?
Dispel this doubt of mine concerning the rising of the virtues of Raghunātha; / tell it to me, who am listening attentively, out of your favor.
Śeṣa said: / Well asked, O highly fortunate one, foremost among the twice-born! / Therefore, hear it directly from me as I speak, with single-minded attention.
Having drunk again and again that nectar of Rāma's arrival flowing from his lotus mouth, / she became bewildered, her limbs rendered motionless—ah!
"Is this a dream of mine, bewildered as I am? Or is it a speech that causes delusion? / For me, ill-fated as I am, how could there be the sight of Rāma again?
By much austerity this infant son was obtained; / and through some sin of mine he fell into separation once again.
O Sumantra, is Rāma well, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa? / How does the hero, dwelling in the forest, remember me, who am so grief-stricken?"

Thus she lamented loudly, having remembered the lord of Raghu's line; / utterly bewildered, she did not perceive anything of her own or of another. / Sumukha too, seeing his mother so exceedingly grieved,
fanned her with the hem of his garment; and she regained consciousness. / He spoke gentle, repeatedly joy-bringing words to the mother;
bringing to mind the arrival of Raghunātha, he made her joyful once more: / "Mother, know that Raghunātha has arrived home, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
and accompanied by Sītā. See them and shower them with blessings!" / Having heard those truthful words spoken by Sumukha,
she attained such joy as I cannot even comprehend. / Rising, she went into the courtyard, the hair on her body bristling with joy;
her limbs trembling with joy, shedding tears, she looked upon Rāma. / Meanwhile, King Rāma, mounted on a palanquin,
prudent as he was, reached the dwelling of his own mother, Kaikeyī, before all others. / Kaikeyī too, bent low under the weight of shame before Rāma standing in front of her,
did not say anything, but fell into great and repeated anxiety. / Rāma, the banner of the Solar dynasty, seeing his mother ashamed,
spoke, consoling her with words filled with modesty. / Śrī Rāma said: / "Mother, having gone to the forest, everything was done by me accordingly.
What else shall I do now by your command, O mother? / Nothing deficient has been done by me; why do you not look at me again?
Welcome him, Bharata, and look at me with blessings!" / Even hearing that speech of his, O sinless one, she, her face cast down,
slowly and softly replied: "Rāma, go to your own abode." / Rāma too, that best among men, having heard the words of his mother,
bowed down and, being a treasure-house of compassion, went to the house of Sumitrā. / Sumitrā, the high-minded, seeing Rāma along with her son,
spoke with blessings, saying: "Live long! Live long!" / And Rāmabhadra, having bowed at his mother's feet
and embraced her with delight, spoke these words again: / "O mother, bearing jewels in your womb, no one has ever done what was done by my brother,
just as this wise one dispelled my grief.
That Sītā, abducted by Rāvaṇa, has been regained by me— / know, mother, that all that is the deed of Lakṣmaṇa!"
Accepting with his head the blessing given by Sumitrā, / he set out for the abode of his own mother, surrounded by the wise.
Seeing his mother thrilled with joy, eager for the sight of him, / Hari quickly descended from his carriage and grasped her feet.
His mother, her mind overwhelmed with longing to see him, / embracing Rāma again and again, attained sheer delight.
Horripilation occurred on her body, and her voice became choked with emotion; / tears of joy, indeed warm, flowed forth as if from a flood of calamity.
Seeing his mother, humble, devoid of her two earrings, / wearing a body destitute of hand ornaments and foot ornaments,
emaciated in limbs, yet slightly delighted by the sight of him, he felt grief; / but thinking, "This is not a time for sorrow," he spoke to her.
Śrī Rāma said: / "Mother, for a long time your feet were not served by me; / therefore, forgive the offense of ill-fated me!
Those sons who are not zealous in the service of their mother and father, / they, O mother, must be considered merely worms born of semen.
What could I do? By our father's command I went to the Daṇḍaka forest; / even there, by the gracious glance of your mercy, I crossed the ocean of sorrow.
Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa and taken to Laṅkā; / by your grace, having slain that lord of the rākṣasas, she was regained by me.
Here is Sītā, devoted to her husband, fallen at your feet; / favor her quickly, bewildered as she is, with her mind placed at your feet!"
Having heard those words, she bestowed blessings / upon that devoted wife, her daughter-in-law who had fallen at her feet, and spoke to her:
"O Sītā, delight for a long time together with your husband, O radiant woman! / Bearing sons, purify your own family, O purifying one!
Women devoted to their husbands like you, who follow the joys and sorrows of their husbands, / do not suffer grief in the three worlds—this is the truth.
O daughter of Videha, by your own self your lineage has been purified by you, / as you followed the pair of Rāma's lotus feet to the great forest.
What wonder is it that men crush millions of enemies, / when in their house there is a virtuous wife desiring what is dear to her husband?"
Having spoken thus to the wife of the lord of Raghu's line, whose eyes were lovely, / she fell silent, delighted, the hair on her body standing on end with joy.
Then his brother Bharata offered up to the wise Rāmacandra / the great kingdom bestowed upon him by his father.
Those ministers, their bodies thrilled with joy, summoned astrologers / skilled in counsel and inquired with supreme reverence for an auspicious moment.
At an auspicious moment, on a favorable day endowed with an auspicious asterism, / they, being ready, performed the consecration to the great kingdom.
Having drawn the earth possessing seven continents upon a beautiful tiger skin, / the king of kings, the great monarch, sat upon it.
From that very day, the minds of the virtuous went to great delight, / while the minds of the wicked, who torment others, became dejected.
Women were devoted to fidelity to their husbands through devotion to their husbands; / never did people commit sin even in their minds, O sage.
Daityas, gods, snakes, yakṣas, asuras, and great serpents— / all, staying on the path of righteousness, bore Rāma's command upon their heads.
They were engaged in helping others, delighted in the happiness of their own duty; / the auspicious moments of day and night were passed in the joys of learning.
Even a strong wind did not forcibly snatch away fine garments / from travelers along the road; no mention was there of thieves.
Rāma was a giver of wealth to supplicants, full of pity, a treasure of compassion; / accompanied by his brothers, he daily offered praise to the guru and gods.

5.5.m: Śeṣa said: / Then the gods, bowing low, their minds gladdened by the slaying of the lord of the daityas named Rāvaṇa, / praised Rāma who had been consecrated.

The gods said: / "Victory, O son of Daśaratha, remover of the distress of the gods! Victory, victory, burner of the race of dānavas! / Victory, destroyer of the enemy whose hands were eager to seize the celestial nymphs!"
Poets are eager to describe that destruction of the lord of demons wrought by you; / but at the cosmic dissolution, Lord of the Universe, you playfully swallow the masses of the worlds again.

Victory, O you freed from the sorrows of birth, old age, and the rest! Powerful one, uplift, uplift! / Victory, O you who took birth in the ocean of the solar dynasty, unaging, immortal, infallible one!
Through the names of you, the supreme deity, even great sinners have been purified; / what then of good people led by excellent twice-borns, who have obtained a fine human body?

We desire in our hearts with devotion the pair of your feet, praised by Hara and Viriñci, / which bestows the fulfillment of desired wishes, adorned with purified marks like the barley-grain and others.

If you, who possess a radiance surpassing the form of the god of love, did not bestow freedom from fear upon the earth, / then how, O compassionate and pure one, could the hosts of gods ever experience happiness again?

Whenever the sons of Danu cause us suffering, then and there may you take birth on earth, / though unborn, imperishable, and supreme Lord, O all-pervading one, assuming your own nature, worshipped by your own.

After covering the surface of the earth with your virtuous deeds resembling the nectar of the dead, destroying sin, / and praised by immortals proclaiming your qualities, return quickly indeed to your own realm.

Beginningless, the foremost, wearing an unaging form, enchanting, crowned, radiant like the god of love— / may he who forcefully struck down his enemies, whose lotus feet are served by the enemy of Smara, bring victory!
Having spoken thus, all those gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, / gratified by the destruction of their enemy, bowed down repeatedly to the leader of Raghu's line.
Exceedingly delighted by this praise, the glorious lord of Raghu's line, / seeing those gods bowed down with their necks bent, spoke:

Śrī Rāma said:
O gods, choose from me some very rare boon, / which no god, demon, or Yakṣa has ever obtained with reverence.

The gods said:
O Lord! Everything supreme has already been obtained by us from the Blessed One, / since this Ten-necked enemy of ours has been slain.
Whenever an Asura inflicts affliction upon us, O Lord, / then and there you must perform just this: the destruction of the enemy.

Having said "So be it," the heroic scion of Raghu spoke again:
Śrī Rāma said:
O gods, listen to my words with reverence:
If a man repeatedly recites, morning or night, even once, / this wonderful hymn composed by you, woven with my qualities,
he will suffer no terrible defeat at the hands of enemies, / nor union with poverty, nor affliction from diseases.
"Indeed, abundant devotion to my pair of feet / shall arise in the joy-filled hearts of men from reciting [this]."
Having spoken thus, that crest-jewel of kings fell silent; / all those gods, greatly delighted, went to their respective worlds.
The lord of the Raghus, protector of the world, protecting his wise brothers, / cherished his subjects as though they were his own sons.
While he ruled, there was no untimely death for the people of the worlds, / nor any defeat through disease and the like, nor great calamity in their homes.
No portents were ever seen, nor any fear arising from an enemy; / the trees were ever fruitful, and the earth abounded in grain.
Their lives were made purposeful, accompanied by sons and grandsons; / their weariness from separation was dispelled by the pleasures born of union with their beloved wives.
They were ever eager for discourse on the lotus feet of the blessed lord of the Raghus; / never did words of censure toward others proceed from them.
Even artisans never conceived sin in their minds—ah!— / as they kept in mind the fear of suffering the strike of the lord of the Raghus' hand.
With their eyes fixed steadily on the sight of Sītā's husband's face, / the people remained constantly filled with compassion.
The kingdom he obtained was without a rival, rich in armies and vehicles, / delightful with joyful and thriving sages and with golden ornaments,
prosperous with those who continually performed the religious duties of sacrifices and public works, / always abounding in crops, and endowed with rich and fertile fields,
a good country, with good subjects, healthy, with good pastures and abundant cattle, / and adorned with rows of temples to the deities;
where the villages were fully supplied, gleaming with wealth and prosperity, / with artificial gardens of beautiful flowers, and trees bearing sweet fruits;
where the lands shone with ponds possessing lotuses; / where only the rivers flowed down from banks, and nowhere was the populace deceitful;
where lineage belonged only to the noble castes and did not mean mere lack of wealth; / where coquetry was found only in women, and never in learned men;

where only the rivers were crooked in their course, and the subjects in that realm were never crooked; / where darkness belonged only to the nights in the dark fortnights, and men were never enveloped in ignorance;
where the quality of passion pertained only to women during menses, and men were not steeped in unrighteousness; / where a person was never blinded by wealth, nor ever lacked food;
where chariot-paths alone were without leading-strings, and royal officials were never lawless; / where the rod was found only in axes, spades, and rows of chowries;
where shades were found only on parasols, and nowhere was anger born of obstruction; / where laments were nowhere heard except among groups of gamblers;
where only dice-players were seen with snares in their hands; / where talk of chill existed only in waters, and weakness only in the waists of women;
where only women possessed firm breasts, and men were not hard-hearted; / where leprosy was found only as a medicinal compounding, and never in a human being;
where perforations were found only in fine gems, and a trident only in sculptors' works; / where trembling arose only from sattva-borne emotions, and never anywhere out of fear;
where fever arose only from desire, and poverty belonged only to sin; / where the rarity of anything was overcome through good fortune, and not through lack of goods;
where only elephants became rutted in battle, and waves rose only in bodies of water; / where the loss of ichor occurred only in elephants, and sharp tips belonged only to thorns;

where separation of strings occurred only in arrows, and strong binding was spoken of only in manuscripts; / where abandonment of affection occurred only toward wicked persons, and never toward one's own people.
He protected that land, cherishing the pampered subjects, / establishing dharma throughout the realm, like the wielder of the rod against the wicked.
As the Lord was thus ruling the land, the surface of the earth, with righteousness, / eleven thousand years passed by.
Then, hearing from a base man of the disrepute of Sītā, / and his own slander from a washerman, the scion of Raghu abandoned her.
As that king was thus ruling the earth with righteousness, / Sītā remained alone, abandoned, yet protected by his command.
Once, as that noble-minded king was seated in the assembly, / there arrived the best of sages, the pot-born great sage.
Taking the respectful offering, the great king rose with Vasiṣṭha / and the assembly to receive the arrival of the one who dried up the ocean.
Welcoming him warmly with hospitality, he inquired of his health; / when he was comfortably seated and rested, the scion of Raghu spoke:

5.6.m:
Śeṣa said:
The wise and heroic teacher of all the worlds spoke to the sage / who was thus delighted by the welcome, a treasure of celibacy and asceticism:
Welcome to you, O highly fortunate one, O pot-born one, O treasure of asceticism! / By the sight of you, indeed all of us with our households are purified.
Does your intellect turn smoothly to the Vedas and Śāstras? / Is there no one on the earth's circle who causes obstruction to your asceticism?
[How is] the highly fortunate Lopāmudrā, who practices dharma / by the power of whose devotion to her husband everything becomes auspicious?
Do tell, O highly fortunate one, embodiment of dharma, treasury of compassion! / What service should I, free from greed, perform for you, O lord of sages?
Through the power of your asceticism everything comes to be in abundance at your will; / nevertheless, showing compassion toward me, speak, O lord of sages!
Śeṣa said: / Thus addressed by the wise king of kings, the teacher of the world, / he spoke to Rāma, the lord of the world, in most humble words.
Agastya said: / O Lord, your sight is exceedingly difficult to attain even for the gods; / knowing this, I have arrived, O king of kings, treasury of compassion!
The demon named Rāvaṇa, a thorn to the world, has been slain by you; / by good fortune the gods are happy today; by good fortune Bibhīṣaṇa is king.
O Rāma, by the sight of you my evil deed has indeed vanished today; / the storehouse of my mind is filled with joy, O best of the gods!
Having spoken thus, the pot-born [sage] at once fell silent, / his mind overcome with the joy of seeing Rāma.
Rāma asked the sage, who was skilled in knowledge, once again: / 'You know everything from all perspectives—past, present, and future, beyond this world.
O sage, tell me everything in great detail as I ask: / Who was that tormentor of the gods, Rāvaṇa, who was slain by me?
Who was Kumbhakarṇa, and what was the caste of that wicked one? / Was he a god, a daitya, a piśāca, or a rākṣasa, O great sage?
Tell me all, O omniscient one, for you know everything in detail; / therefore, out of compassion toward me, tell me everything.'
Having heard those words, the pot-born [sage], a treasure of asceticism, / set about to explain that which had been asked by the king of Raghu's line.
'O king, Brahmā is the creator, and Pulastya was his son; / from him was born Viśravas, skilled in the knowledge of the Vedas.
He had two wives, who upheld the conduct of devotion to their husband: / one named Mandākinī, and the second is known as Kaikasī.
On the first was born Dhanada, possessing the splendor of a guardian of the world, / who, by the grace of Śiva, established his residence in Laṅkā.
On the daughter of Vidyunmālin, however, three great sons were born: / Rāvaṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, and the virtuous Bibhīṣaṇa.
Because of their birth from the womb of a rākṣasa woman, and taking place at twilight, / two of them possessed minds adept in unrighteousness, O wise one!
Once, mounting the Puṣpaka aerial chariot, very splendid, / fashioned of gold, adorned with garlands of little tinkling bells,
[Dhanada] went to see his parents, endowed with splendor, / praised by his retinues, and decorated with various gems.
Having arrived, that son fell at the feet of his parents for a long time, / his mind overwhelmed with joy, the hair of his body standing on end.
He said: "Today is an auspicious day for me, the dawn of the fruit of great fortune, / since your feet, the sight of which yields great merit, have been seen by me."
Having praised him with these and other verses of praise, he went to his own abode; / his parents also were filled with joy out of affection for their son.
Seeing him, the intelligent Rāvaṇa said to his mother: / "Who is this man—a god, a yakṣa, or an excellent human—
who, having served the feet of my father, has departed again, / a treasury of great fortune, well surrounded by his attendants?
By what asceticism did he obtain this aerial chariot moving with the speed of wind, / an excellent place for dalliance, sports, and gardens?"
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech, the mother, perturbed with anger, / dejected and rolling her eyes somewhat, spoke to her son:
"O son, listen to my words full of many teachings, / excelling in discerning the birth, deeds, and other matters of this one.
A dispensation born of the womb of my co-wife has appeared, / by whom the pure, great lineage of his mother has been illuminated.
You, however, are a worm born from my womb, a sinner who only fills his own belly; / just as a donkey knows its own load but not its qualities,
so you are seen to be ignorant, indulging in sleeping, sitting, and pleasure; / asleep, wandering, and fallen somewhere—such alone is your existence.
By him, through asceticism pleasing to Śiva, was obtained / the residence in Laṅkā, the aerial chariot swift as thought, and the fortune of a kingdom.
Truly fortunate is his mother, very lucky and of great prosperity, / whose son, through his own virtues, has attained the status of the great!"
Hearing what had been spoken in anger by his distressed mother, the best among the wicked-minded, / restraining his anger within himself, again spoke words to her, resolute regarding asceticism:
Rāvaṇa said: / "O mother, listen to my words full of pride! / You alone are the mother of gems, whose sons the three of us are!
What is that worm, that Dhanada? What is that puny asceticism of his? / What is that kingdom of Laṅkā, attended by few servants?
O compassionate mother, listen to my vow born of zeal, / a vow never made by any doer, O highly fortunate Kaikasī!
If I do not bring the entire world under control / by severe asceticisms that cause the satisfaction of Brahmā,
constantly abandoning food, water, sleep, and play— / then may I incur the sin of slaying the realm of the ancestors!"
Kumbhakarṇa, together with Vibhīṣaṇa, also made [that vow]; / having spoken thus with his brother Rāvaṇa, he went to the mountain forest.

5.7.m: Agastya said: / Then that demon performed fierce asceticism for ten thousand years, / gazing at the sun with his eyes while standing on one foot.
Kumbhakarṇa also performed extremely severe asceticism, / and the righteous Vibhīṣaṇa practiced supreme asceticism.
Then the blessed lord Prajāpati, the god of gods, / served by the crowns of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and others, was pleased.
He granted a very great kingdom illuminating the three worlds, / and made his body handsome, served by gods and dānavas.
Then his righteous brother Dhanada was tormented, / and by force his aerial chariot and the city of Laṅkā were taken from him.
The entire world was tormented, and the gods fled to heaven; / he killed the family of brāhmaṇas, a destroyer of sages from their root.
Then the gods, extremely distressed, approached Brahmā together with Indra; / those great-souled ones offered praise and prostrated like a staff.
All those gods praised him with respectful, suppliant words; / then the blessed lord, being pleased, said, "What shall I do?"
Then the gods reported before Brahmā / the affliction caused by the Ten-necked one and their own defeat.
Having meditated for a moment, Brahmā went to Kailāsa with the gods; / at the side of that mountain, bewildered by the marvels,
the gods, with Śakra at their head, stood and praised Śambhu: / "Salutations to Bhava, to Śarva, salutations to you with a blue neck!
Salutations to the gross one, to the subtle one, salutations to you who have manifold forms!" / Hearing this speech uttered by every mouth, Śaṅkara
said to Nandin: "Bring the gods near me." / Meanwhile, those gods, having been summoned by Nandin,
entered the inner chamber and saw [him] with astonished eyes; / then Brahmā, having arrived, beheld Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
[Śaṃkara] served by thousands of crores of attendants full of joy, / naked, misshapen, crooked, dusty, and formidable.
Prostrating and standing in front along with the gods, the Grandfather [Brahmā] / said to the Lord of gods: “Look upon the condition of the celestials!
Have mercy, O Mahādeva, lover of those who seek refuge! / Make an effort to slay the wicked Daitya, O Lord!”
Hearing that speech of his, filled with wretchedness and sorrow, / he too, together with all the thirty [gods], went to Hari's abode.
All the sages praised [him], along with the gods, Uragas, and Kinnaras: / “Victory, O Mādhava, Lord of gods! Victory, O dispeller of the distress of devoted people!
Look upon, O Mahādeva, look upon your own servants!” / Thus all the gods, led by Śarva, shouted aloud.

Hearing what was said, Viṣṇu, the supreme lord of the gods, having seen the distress of the gods and reflected [upon it], / spoke to the gods in a voice deep as a thundercloud, as if calming their sorrow:

“O immortals led by Brahmā, Śarva, and Indra, listen to my words devoted to your welfare! / I know the fear caused for you by the Ten-necked one [Rāvaṇa]; taking an incarnation now, I shall destroy it.

The city of Ayodhyā, protected by kings born in the solar dynasty / who performed righteous deeds such as great gifts and sacrifices, an ornament to the earth's surface, shines with grounds of silver.
In it, King Daśaratha, childless [yet] endowed with prosperity, / the all-powerful ruler who has conquered the circle of the quarters, now protects the kingdom.
Begged [by him] out of desire for sons from the venerable Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, / he, endowed with great strength, sacrificed in the rite for obtaining a son according to the rules.
Then I was formerly petitioned by him through his penance, O gods; / through affection, I [shall be born] fourfold in his three wives for your sake.
Endowed with the names Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Śatrughna, and Bharata, / I will accomplish the eradication of Rāvaṇa along with his roots, army, and mounts.
You also, descending with your own portions, must roam here, / in the form of bears and monkeys everywhere upon the face of the earth.”
Having spoken thus, O sage, the voice that had arisen in the sky immediately ceased; / having heard that great proclamation, all the gods were glad at heart.
They did just as was spoken by the wise God of gods: / the earth was filled with their own portions in the form of bears and monkeys.
That very Viṣṇu, the great god who destroys the sorrow of the gods, / is none other than you, O great king, the Lord who assumed a body.
This Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, O wise one, / [are also your portions]; and from your portion, the Ten-necked one, the tormentor of the gods, was born.
Due to the continuance of former enmity, he abducted Jānakī again; / he, a Daitya belonging to the race of Brahmarākṣasas, was slain by you.
The son of Pulastya, the lord of Daityas, the sole thorn to all the worlds, / was struck down; the entire earth obtained happiness, O Maheśvara!
Now there is happiness for Brāhmaṇas, strength of asceticism for sages; / auspicious are all sacred bathing places, and all sacrifices are properly performed.
While you are king, the whole world, along with gods, Asuras, and human beings, / has attained happiness, O Soul of all, Womb of the universe, Best of men!
All this has been recounted to you, which I was asked by you, O sinless one, / both his origin and his downfall, according to my understanding.”

Hearing thus the news relating to the lineage of the lord of the sons of Diti, the Supreme Person, the Sovereign and Ruler, / his lotus-face flowing with tears from choked-up weeping, his power renowned, fell to the ground in the assembly.

5.8.m: Śeṣa said: / O Vātsyāyana, best of sages, [such is] the sin-destroying story / of the God of gods who is favorable to Brāhmaṇas, the sole protector of all dharma.
Seeing the king fainted, the pot-born [Agastya], a treasury of asceticism, / gently touched his tears with his hand and spoke:
“O Rāma, take heart quickly! Why do you sink down into despair? / You are the destroyer of the Daitya race, the eternal Mahāviṣṇu.
The past, the future, and the present, the immobile and mobile world— / without you, there is no mover; why have you fainted here?”
Hearing the words spoken by the pot-born [sage], the great king / arose, his handsome face filled with tears flowing from his eyes.
And he spoke very wretchedly, in full, distinct words, / his form bent with the weight of shame, turning his face away in horror from offending Brāhmaṇas.
The auspicious Rāma said: / “Ah, behold the ignorance of me, a bewildered, wicked soul, / in that, greedy with desire, I killed one who grew up in a Brāhmaṇa family!
For the sake of a woman, I, [though] possessing discernment of the Vedas and Śāstras, / killed a Brāhmaṇa; destitute of intellect, I am extremely wicked-minded.
In the family of the Ikṣvākus, no Brāhmaṇa ever met with harsh words; / by performing such an act, it has been utterly stained by me.
Those Brāhmaṇas who are worthy of worship through gifts, honors, and food— / those Brāhmaṇas were slain by me with volleys of assembled arrows.
To what worlds shall I go? Even Kumbhīpāka is intolerable! / There is no such sacred bathing place that is capable of purifying me.
Neither sacrifice, nor asceticism, nor gifts, nor vows and the like / can truly deliver and purify me, a harmer of Brāhmaṇas!
The men bound for hell by whom the Brāhmaṇa family was angered— / those men, having gone to hell, will experience sorrow abundantly.
The Vedas are the root of the dharmas of those who discern castes and stages of life, / and the root of those [Vedas] is the Brāhmaṇa family, the sole branches of all the Vedas.
For me, the cutter of that root through arrogance, what world shall I experience? / What is indeed to be done today by which there may be welfare for me?”
Śeṣa said: / To Rāma, the king of kings, the bull of Raghu's line, who had taken an illusory human body, / as he lamented vehemently, the pot-born [sage] spoke these words.
Agastya said: / “Do not grieve, O greatly steadfast king, O highly intelligent one! / You could not incur the killing of a Brāhmaṇa when desiring the destruction of the wicked.
You are the ancient Person directly, the Lord beyond material nature, / the creator, destroyer, protector, witness, devoid of qualities, yet possessing qualities by your own will.
A drinker of liquor, a killer of a Brāhmaṇa, a stealer of gold, a committer of great sins— / all indeed become quickly purified by the utterance of your name.
This Queen, the daughter of Janaka, is the great knowledge [Mahāvidyā], O highly intelligent one, / by merely remembering whom the liberated will go to the auspicious path.
Rāvaṇa was not truly a Daitya; he was your servant in Vaikuṇṭha; / he attained the status of a Daitya due to a curse of sages, O destroyer of Danujas!
You were the bestower of favor upon him, and not the slayer of a twice-born. / Considering this, you should not grieve any more for your own deed.”
Having heard those words, Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, / spoke sweet words uttered with a faltering voice:

The auspicious Rāma said: / “Sin is said to be of two kinds according to the distinction of intentional and unintentional: / that which is done deliberately is intentional, while that which is devoid of intention is unintentional.
An act done deliberately is destroyed only by experiencing its fruit; / other [acts] may be destroyed by remorse; this is settled by the Śāstras.
For me, who performed the highly censured murder of a Brāhmaṇa deliberately, / praise of the virtuous is not agreeable to dispel my grief.
Tell me of something that burns away sin, / whether a vow, a gift, a sacrifice, a sacred bathing place, or a great rite of worship.”
by which my spotless fame will indeed purify the worlds / that have incurred pollution from wicked conduct and whose luster has been destroyed by the slaughter of a Brahmin."
Śeṣa said: / To that Rāma who spoke thus, he who was a treasury of austerities, / whose feet were illuminated by the crest-jewels of bowing gods and demons, spoke:
"Listen, Rāma, mighty hero, author of grace upon the world, / to the word that I speak to you for removing the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He crosses over all sin who indeed performs the horse sacrifice; / therefore, O Soul of the Universe, sacrifice with the splendid horse sacrifice.
The sacrifice of seven threads is to be accomplished by you, a wise ruler of the earth, / endowed with great prosperity, exceedingly distinguished in great strength."
That horse sacrifice destroys the sin of killing brāhmaṇas, / which the great king Dilīpa, your ancestor, performed.
Śatakratu, that bull among men, having performed a hundred sacrifices, / attained the station in Amarāvatī thoroughly attended by gods and Daityas.
Manu, King Sagara, Marutta, and the son of Nahuṣa— / all these ancestors attained [their] station after performing the sacrifice.
Therefore perform [it], O chief of kings; you are capable in every respect. / Your brothers, resembling guardians of the worlds, are dedicated to your welfare."

Hearing what the sage had said, that fortunate best of Raghu's line, fearing the slaying of a brāhmaṇa / and wishing to perform a sacrifice with noble intent, asked about the rite celebrated by those who know the past.

5.9.m: Glorious Rāma said: / "What kind of horse should be had there? What is the rite for its worship? / How can it be performed, and who are the enemies to be conquered there?"
Agastya said: / "Auspicious in body, with a colour resembling the water of the Gaṅgā, / dark in the ears, red in the face, yellow in the tail, with good marks,
fleet as thought, swift in every direction, equal in splendour to Uccaiḥśravas— / such is the horse declared for the horse sacrifice, endowed with auspicious marks.
Having worshipped it according to rule on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha, / and having written on its forehead a plate marked with one's name and might,
it should be released with effort, guarded by protectors. / Wherever the sacrificial horse goes, there the protector should go.
If someone binds it by force, proud of his own prowess and might, / from him the horse must be brought back forcibly by the protectors.
Meanwhile, the performer must remain here under observances according to proper rule, / holding a deer's horn and observing celibacy.
While he observes the vow until the year elapses, / during that time the poor, the blind, and the miserable should be satisfied with wealth and other gifts.
Food should be given copiously, or abundant wealth, O noble one; / whatever a wise man requests, that very thing he gives.
When the rite is performed in this manner, the sacrifice reaches completion / and brings about the destruction of all sins, O destroyer of foes.
Therefore you are capable in performing, maintaining, and worshipping; / having made your fame spotless, purify other people, O king."
Glorious Rāma said: / "Look now, O best of the twice-born, into my stable: / are there such horses endowed with auspicious marks, or not?"
Having heard those words, Agastya, an ocean of compassion, / arose, examining auspicious horses fit for the sacrifice.
Having gone then to the stable together with Rāmacandra, / he saw horses of varied limbs, fleet as thought, of great strength.

"Are these descended from the king of horses, arrived on the surface of the earth, or the massed fame of the lords of Raghu gathered in one place? / Or is this an ocean of nectar in the form of horses?"—thinking thus within his mind, the sage was filled with wonder as he looked.
On one side was an excellent row of red-bodied horses; / on another, horses with dark ears, radiant with the luster of musk;
on one side horses of golden hue, and on another those of dark-blue color; / on one side surrounded by horses distinguished by dapple colors.
Thus looking at all of them, his mind filled with curiosity, / the sage went to another place to see the horses fit for sacrifice.
He saw there hundreds bound of that very colour; / having seen them, that sage attained wonder, his limbs thrilled with joy.
On one side were those with dark ears, resembling milk with all their limbs, / yellow-tailed, red in the face, endowed with auspicious marks.

Gazing all around at those faultless horses, resembling the flow of spotless water, graced with speed like thought, resplendent like a heap of pure fame, / the sage who dried up the ocean, his face and eyes thrilled with brilliance at the sight of the extraordinary horses, spoke to Sītā's husband:
Agastya said: / "Looking at your many auspicious steeds fit for the horse sacrifice, / today my eyes know no satiation, O best of Raghus.
O Rāmacandra, highly fortunate one, bowed to by gods and asuras, / perform the horse sacrifice, O great king, in full detail.

Like the lord of the gods, about to perform all the hosts of sacrifices, drying up the enemy of the deities like the sun [dries] water, / having conquered in battle the chief of the host of slain foes, enjoy this happiness on the face of the earth, O greatly fortunate one!"
With all his senses delighted by such discourse, / he brought together all the charming materials for the sacrifice.
Accompanied by the sage, the great king arrived at the bank of the Sarayū; / he ploughed the vast ground with golden ploughs.
Having marked out the ground measuring four yojanas in many ways, / that best of men erected pavilions for the sacrifice.
Having made the sacrificial pit according to rule, endowed with the vulva-shaped rim, / constructed with many gems, endowed with all splendours,
the lord of sages, the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha of very great asceticism, / had all that executed in accordance with the injunctions of the Vedas and treatises.
Disciples sent by that sage went to the hermitages of the foremost sages / and announced the best of Raghus undertaking the horse sacrifice.
Invited then, all the ṛṣis, the foremost of ascetics, / came, intensely eager for the sight of the supreme lord.
Nārada, the one named Asita, Parvata, the sage Kapila, / Jātūkarṇya, Aṅgiras, Vyāsa, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, Atri, Āsuri,
Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Saṃvarta, and the one named Śuka— / these and others went to the excellent horse sacrifice of Rāma.
The king of Raghu's line, high-minded, honoured all of them / by rising to meet them, salutations, water for hospitality, seats, and the like.
He whose prowess had often been witnessed gave them cattle and gold: / "Great indeed is my fortune today, since you have come to [my] sight."
Śeṣa said: / "When the gathering of foremost ṛṣis was thus assembled, O brāhmaṇa, / there arose, oh!, discussion on dharma highly agreed upon for the castes and stages of life."
Vātsyāyana said: / "What discussion on dharma was there, or what wondrous thing was spoken? / What indeed did the virtuous say out of compassion for all the worlds?"
Śeṣa said: / "Seeing those assembled sages, the great Rāma, son of Daśaratha, / asked about all the dharmas appropriate for all castes and stages of life.
Questioned by Rāma, they declared the dharmas of great merit; / I shall proclaim them all to you: listen to them according to rule."
The ṛṣis said: / "Sacrificing, studying, and the like should always be performed by a brāhmaṇa; / having read the Vedas, free from passion, he should never enter the householder's life.
Service to the low and dependent living should always be abandoned by a brāhmaṇa; / even when fallen into misfortune, he should never live by a dog's livelihood.
Approaching [one's wife] during the fertile period is the supreme dharma of a householder; / remembering the boon granted to women, or he should desire offspring.
Approaching [one's wife] by day is considered by men to shorten life; / the day of a śrāddha and all sacred transition days must be avoided by the wise man.
If he approaches a woman then through delusion, he falls from the supreme dharma. / He who approaches [his wife] during the fertile period and is devoted to his own wife
is to be known as a perpetual celibate, even though living in the stage of a householder. / The fertile period consists of sixteen nights; four among them are censured.
Among them, even [nights] grant sons, uneven grant daughters; / having avoided an inauspicious moon, and having left aside Maghā and Mūla,
being pure, one should approach one's wife, especially under a constellation of masculine name; / she will give birth to a pure son, an achiever of the aims of human life.
"In the ārṣa marriage, that which is declared as a pair of cattle is praised; / but taking even a minute bride-price for a maiden makes the buyer of a maiden an evildoer."
Commerce, serving a king, non-study of the Vedas, / a bad marriage, and omission of religious acts are causes of the downfall of a family.
Either with food, water, milk, roots, or fruits, a householder [may honor guests]; / but as for the merit gained through the gift of a cow according to rule to a worthy recipient,
from whose house an unhonored guest departs disappointed in hope, / he is instantly cast out from the merit accumulated since birth.
A householder should eat the nectar after offering to the ancestors, gods, and men; / he who cooks for his own sake eats sin, merely filling his own belly.
On the sixth and eighth [lunar days], sin always enters into oil and meat; / likewise, on the fourteenth and the new moon, one should avoid a razor and women.
One should not have intercourse with a menstruating woman, nor eat together with one's wife; / one should not eat dressed in a single garment, nor eat on a raised seat.
A best of men desiring vigor should not look at a woman while she is eating; / one should not blow on fire with one's mouth, nor look upon a naked woman.
One should not warm one's feet at a fire, nor throw an impure thing [into it]; / one should not commit violence against living beings, nor eat at the two twilights.
One should not point out a cow suckling [a calf], nor show a rainbow; / nor should one eat food from which the essence has departed by day, nor curd at night.
One should not greet a woman during her period, nor eat to full satiety at night; / one should not be overly fond of music and dance, nor wash one's feet in a bronze vessel.
One should not wear clothing or sandals used by another; / one should not eat from a broken vessel, nor eat spoiled food.
One should not go to bed with wet feet, nor go anywhere while impure with food remnants; / nor should one eat lying down, nor touch one's head while impure with food remnants.
One should not praise a man, nor despise oneself; / one should not bow to one who is raised in pride, nor speak of others' secret faults.
Having thus taken refuge in the householder stage, one should go to the forest-dwelling stage, / with one's wife or having abandoned one's wife, and thereafter become detached.
These and other duties declared by the sages at that time / were heard by the great Rāma, who desired the welfare of all the world.

5.10.m: Śeṣa said: / As he was thus listening to the duties, spring arrived, / when the commencement of sacrificial rites and the like by great-souled ones [takes place].
Seeing that time, the wise Vasiṣṭha, [along with] the jar-born [Agastya], / spoke appropriately to the great king Rāmacandra.
Vasiṣṭha said: / "O mighty-armed Rāmacandra, your time has arrived / when the horse, fully worshiped, should be released for the sacrifice.
Let the provisions be prepared there; let the best of the twice-born be summoned; / let the Blessed Lord perform the proper worship of the Brahmins.
Let him give gifts that arise in his mind to the poor, the blind, and the destitute, / according to rule, having honored and shown high respect to them.
Consecrated here with your good golden wife, perform the vow: / sleeping on the ground, celibate, devoid of enjoyments and wealth,
bearing a deer horn, wearing a girdle, a black-antelope skin, and a staff at your waist; / let him prepare the equipment of the sacrifice, complete with all materials."
Having heard these profound and true words of Vasiṣṭha, / the wise one spoke to Lakṣmaṇa [words] rich in various meanings:
The glorious Rāma said: / "Listen, Lakṣmaṇa, to my word, and having heard it, execute it quickly: / bring with effort a horse suitable for the rite of the horse sacrifice."
Śeṣa said: / Having heard the word of the lord of the Raghus, Lakṣmaṇa, conqueror of enemies, / then addressed these words of varied descriptions to the commander of the army.
Make ready the army whose powerful divisions surge with the force of death and the storm-wind, / equipped with excellent chariots, elephants, foot soldiers, and mounted on fine steeds.
Let horses swift as the wind be readied, their hoof-falls charming as rows of waves, / mounted by excellent riders bearing many weapons, striking at the enemy host.

Let elephants resembling mountains be viewed, with mahouts holding spears and javelins in their hands, / brave, armed, offering abundant gifts of temporal secretions, intoxicated, filled with all sorts of weapons and missiles.

Let my chariots, shining with extensive and manifold riches, yoked to horses swift as the wind, / whose upper decks are filled with weapons and missiles that bring to mind the destruction of various enemies, be brought by hosts of charioteers.
Let foot-soldiers by the hundreds come to me with missiles and fire in their hands, / their efforts fully applied to guarding the horse worthy of the horse sacrifice."
Hearing these words of the noble Lakṣmaṇa, / the general named Kālajit made preparations.

Adorned with the ten stable marks, endowed with the beauty of light and fine hair, having a distinct conch-like throat, a jewel in the expanse of its neck-band, / bearing a white luster on its face and a black luster on its ears, the horse shone then, holding a cluster of reins at the tips of hands.
With its face adorned with ornaments, shining with sparkling jewels, / adorned with garlands of pearls, the horse set forth.
Sheltered by a white parasol, adorned with white fly-whisks, / its body surrounded by great beauty, the king of horses then set forth.
In front, in the middle, and behind were the soldiers, / just as gods formerly attended Hari with suitable service.
Then, having assembled the whole army, he issued orders to all of it, / teeming with vast multitudes of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers.
Then from here and there the sound of the gathering armies was heard; / then the roar of kettle-drums arose in that best of cities.
By that great sound beloved of heroes, / the mountain peaks trembled and palaces shook.
There was a great sound of neighing from the bewildered horses, O king; / resounded by the impact of chariot wheels, the earth seemed to quake.
And the earth was covered on all sides by marching herds of elephants; / the dust rising there brought about the disappearance of the people.
The great army, covering the sun with parasols, / advanced, teeming with people, dispatched by the commander named Kālajit.
Roaring, the foremost warriors, stirring up martial excitement, / set out with joy, prepared for the sacrifice of Raghunātha.

Applying musk-fragrant unguent to their limbs, their heads adorned with pure garlands of flowers, / their entire bodies decorated with crowns and bracelets, all of them departed, dispatched by the lord of the earth.
In this manner, O great king, those excellent warriors of the army went forth: / bow-wielders, noose-bearers, and sword-bearers, marching in distinct ranks.
Thus, by and by, the horse reached the pavilion marked out for the sacrifice, / striking the surface of the earth with its hooves and leaping toward the sky.
Seeing that the horse had arrived, Rāma, his heart greatly pleased, / urged Vasiṣṭha toward performing the rituals.
Vasiṣṭha, having summoned Rāma along with his golden wife, / had him undertake the rite that removes the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa.
Observing the vow of celibacy and taking hold of a deer horn, / Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, had that ritual performed.
A sacrificial pit proportionate to the pavilion was prepared for the rite; / the wise preceptor there, versed in the reflection on the Vedas and śāstras,
was Vasiṣṭha, the ancestral family teacher of Raghunātha, the sage. / O brāhmaṇa, Agastya, a treasure of austerity, acted there as the brahmā priest.
The sage Vālmīki was the adhvaryu priest, while the sage Kaṇva was the doorkeeper. / There were eight auspicious gates, endowed with archways.
At every gate, O brāhmaṇa, stood a pair of brāhmaṇas learned in the supreme mantras. / At the eastern gate were the two excellent sages named Devala and Asita.
At the southern gate were the two treasures of austerity, Kaśyapa and Atri, possessed of majesty. / At the western gate were the two ṛṣis, Jātūkarṇya and Jājali.
At the northern gate were two ascetics, the sages Dvita and Ekata. / Having thus arranged the rules for the gates, Vasiṣṭha and the pot-born [Agastya],
began to perform the proper worship of the excellent horse, O twice-born. / Auspicious married women there, adorned with garments and ornaments,

worshipped the revered [horse] with turmeric, unbroken rice grains, scents, and other offerings; / then, having waved lights before it and fumigated it with incense under the watchful eyes of the elders,
courtesans then performed congratulations by command of the brāhmaṇas. / Having thus worshipped it, upon its spotlessly clear forehead anointed with sandalwood,
rich with fragrances like saffron and endowed with all beauty, / he bound a radiant plate made of refined gold.
On it, he inscribed the mighty glory and strength of the son of Daśaratha: / "The banner of the Solar dynasty, the archer, the guru of the initiation into the bow,
before whom all gods together with the asuras bow with their jeweled diadems— / his son, the upholder of Raghu’s line, takes away the arrogance of warriors' strength.
Illustrious Rāmacandra, the crest-jewel of all heroes, / born of the womb of his mother, the wife of the king of Kosala,
the jewel born of her womb, Rāma, the destroyer of foes, / well-instructed by a brāhmaṇa, is performing a horse sacrifice
to dispel the sin of slaying the eminent brāhmaṇa named Rāvaṇa. / By him this chief of mounts, the best of horses, has been released.
Protected by trenches consisting of an army of immense might, / its guardian is his brother Śatrughna, the slayer of Lavaṇa,
accompanied by host of troops consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. / If any king has the haughty pride arising from the intoxication of his own strength:
'We are bowmen, we are heroes, we are supreme and fierce here,' / let them seize by force this mount adorned with a necklace of jewels,
swift as thought, speedy as desire, radiant above all locomotion. / Then [my] brother Śatrughna will effortlessly free the horse

with calf-toothed arrows, sharp-pointed, discharged from his bow."

These and other things the chief of great sages wrote, / [recording] the radiant majesty of the strength of glorious Rāmabhadra's arms.
[He] released [the horse], a store of beauty, extremely swift with the speed of the wind, / whose special course extended across the subterranean realm and the earth.
Then Rāma, the best of weapon-bearers, commanded Śatrughna: / "Go behind the horse that wanders at will, in order to guard it.
Go, O Śatrughna, along the horse’s path; may good fortune be yours! / May your two arms, O tormentor of enemies, be victorious over foes!

Whatever warriors confront you in battle must be checked by you; protect the horse on this great earth, endowed with your multitude of virtues. / Those who are sleeping, fallen, devoid of garments, terrified, and bowing low—do not strike them, so that righteous men may praise your action.
Those who are deprived of chariots, alarmed with fear, and who say, 'We are yours,' / are never to be killed by you, O Śatrughna, as one desiring merit.
Whoever slays one who is sober, one who is intoxicated, one who is asleep, one who is submerged, one afflicted with terror, / or one saying, 'I am yours,' goes to the lowest destination.
Do not direct your mental inclination toward the property of others or toward another's wife; / do not take pleasure in what is base, being full of all good virtues.
Do not incite the elders first; be victorious in battle; / do not transgress the honor due to those worthy of honor, remaining endowed with compassion.
Bow to a cow, a brāhmaṇa, and a Vaiṣṇava devoted to dharma; / having paid homage, wherever you go, there you will attain success.
Viṣṇu is the lord of all, the witness, the all-pervading embodiment; / those who belong to him, O mighty-armed one, wander about indeed possessing his form.
Those who remember Mahāviṣṇu dwelling in the hearts of all beings / are to be considered of the same form as Mahāviṣṇu, O upholder of Raghu’s line.
He to whom no one is his own and no one is an alien, to whom an enemy is equal to a friend— / such Vaiṣṇavas purify a sinner in an instant.
Those to whom the Bhāgavata is dear, and to whom brāhmaṇas are dear, / have been sent here from Vaikuṇṭha for the purpose of purifying the world.
He in whose mouth is the name of Hari, in whose heart is the eternal Viṣṇu, / and in whose belly is the food offered to Viṣṇu, is a Vaiṣṇava, even if he were an outcaste.
Those to whom the Vedas are dearest and not pleasure born of worldly existence, / and who are devoted to their own duty—bow down to them, endowed with humility.
For those who see no difference between Śiva and Viṣṇu, nor between Brahmā and Maheśvara, / I carry on my head the dust of their feet, which is pure and destroys sins.
He for whom Gaurī, Gaṅgā, and Mahālakṣmī are not distinct— / all such men should be considered to have arrived here from heaven.
He who protects those who take refuge, who is dedicated to honoring and giving, / according to his capacity, for the pleasure of Hari—he is to be known as the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
He whose name swiftly burns away a great mass of sins— / one who has devotion to his pair of feet is a Vaiṣṇava.
Those whose senses are under control and whose mind meditates on Hari— / by bowing to them, one is purified from birth until death.

Renouncing another man's wife like a sword's edge, you will become the vessel of glory, ornament, and prosperity; / thus following my instruction, you will attain the supreme abode, praiseworthy through proper union."

5.11.m: Śeṣa said: / Having thus instructed him, the blessed Rāma, the tormentor of enemies, / looking again at the warriors, spoke with auspicious words:
"Behind my brother Śatrughna, who protects the horse, / who will go, guarding [him] and obeying his commands?"

"Let him who can conquer all the champion warriors that advance against him / with salvos of weapons piercing the vitals, take this betel roll from my hand, / spreading his wide renown upon the earth!"
When Rāma had spoken thus, Puṣkala, the son of Bharata, / took the betel leaf from the lotus-hand of the king of Raghu's line.
"My lord, I shall go, guarding Śatrughna's rear day by day, / fully armored, bearing all weapons and missiles, bow and arrows, O master!
Today your majesty alone will conquer the entire surface of the earth; / we are merely instruments, O wise Rāmacandra!
By your grace, even if the whole world, along with gods, asuras, and humans, / should stand ready for battle, I am truly able to ward them off.
The master will know everything from witnessing my prowess; / here I go, to act as the rear guard for Śatrughna."
To Bharata's son who spoke thus, praising him, approving with ‘Excellent!’, / Lord Hari addressed all the monkey chiefs, foremost among whom was the son of the Wind:
[Rāma said:] "O Hanūmat, mighty hero, listen respectfully to my words: / by your grace I obtained this kingdom free of thorns.
When you crossed the ocean for my reunion with Sītā— / I know all of that deed of yours, O monkey king, O Hari!
Go by my command, being the guardian of my army; / my brother Śatrughna is to be protected just like myself.
Wherever Śatrughna suffers any lapse of mind, / there you, O wise one, must instruct my brother.’
Hearing these great words of the wise Rāmacandra, / he placed them on his head and then made an obeisance.
Then the great king commanded Jāmbavat, the monkey lord, / supreme in splendour among monkeys, to serve Raghunātha:
Aṅgada, Gavaya, Mainda, and the monkey Dadhimukha, / Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, Śatabali, and the two monkeys Akṣika [and Dvivida],
Nīla, Nala, Manovega, Adhigantṛ, and the son of a monkey— / all of you, headed by these, be prepared!
Adorned with all the elephants and fine horses with ornaments of refined gold, / equipped with armour and helmets, let them set forth swiftly.’

Śeṣa said: / Having summoned Sumantra, his excellent counselor, Rāma, radiant with strength and valor, then said: / ‘Crown of ministers, tell me which men are able to protect the horse here and should be appointed?’
Hearing what he had said, he who was a slayer of enemy heroes spoke / of the kings here who were strong and capable of guarding the horse:
‘O Raghunātha, listen to these nine well-prepared heroes, / archers endowed with great learning, skilled in all weapons and missiles:
The foremost in valor, Nīlaratna, and King Lakṣmīnidhi, / Riputāpa, Ugrahaya, and the king skilled in weapons—
this warrior Nīlaratna is a great hero, a leader among charioteers; / he alone can protect a hundred thousand, and fight a hundred thousand without fear.
Let him go to guard the horse with ten akṣauhiṇīs, / armored, wearing helmets, [like] my own upraised arms.
This Pratāpāgrya, who has crushed the pride of his foes, / is a shooter of arrows with both left and right hands, the best knower of all missiles.
Let this young warrior, bearing the rod of his bow, fully armed for the destruction of foes, / go to guard the sacrificial horse with twenty akṣauhiṇīs.
Likewise, let Lakṣmīnidhi, the best of warriors, go— / he who, having propitiated Brahmā through penance, mastered missiles:
The Brahmā missile, the Pāśupata missile, the Gāruḍa, the one named Nāga, / the Māyūra, the Nākula, the Raudra, the Vaiṣṇava, the one called Megha,
the Vajra, the one called Pārvata, and likewise the one named Vāyavya— / he knows the employment and discharge of missiles such as these.
Accompanied by a single akṣauhiṇī of his own troops, / let this crown of heroes, shatterer of all enemies, march forth.
