Let this Riputāpa, foremost of archers, also go today, / skilled in all weapons and missiles, a forest fire to the lineage of foes.
Let him march with a vast fourfold army; / let these mighty heroes today carry Śatrughna’s command on their heads!"
The great king Ugrāśva as well, and this one skilled in weaponry— / let them all depart fully armoured, as guardians of your horse.’
Hearing what was spoken by the minister, he rejoiced, / and ordered those warriors mentioned by Sumantra.
Receiving Raghunātha's permission, they were filled with joy, / desiring war for a long time, arrogant in battle.
Equipped with armor and other gear, and with the practice of weapons and missiles, / they went to Śatrughna's residence, urged on by the lord of Sītā.
Śeṣa said: / Then, instructed by the sage, Rāma worshipped in order according to rule / the preceptor and all the sages, with the best of sacrificial gifts as prescribed.
Rāma gave to the preceptor an elephant sixty years old, / a horse swift as thought adorned with a garland of jewels,
and a golden chariot adorned with gems and jewels, / yoked with four steeds and equipped with all implements.
a hundred thousand visible gems, a hundred scales of pearls, / and a thousand scales of corals of radiant brilliance;
a prosperous village teeming with diverse people, / yielding various crops and filled with diverse mansions.
He gave likewise to the Brahmā priest, and he gave to the Hotṛ and to the Adhvaryu; / having given lavishly to the priests, the best of the Raghus bowed down.
All of them, honored, offered various words of blessing: / ‘Live long, O great king, Rāmacandra, descendant of Raghu!’
[He gave] gifts of maidens, gifts of land, gifts of elephants as well, / gifts of horses, gifts of gold, and gifts of sesame seeds together with pearls.
the gift of food, the gift of milk, the supreme gift of safety, / and gifts of all gems, the great [king] commanded to the brāhmaṇas.
‘Give, give! Give wealth! Say “no” to no one! / Let food be given, let food be given, accompanied by all luxuries!’
Thus the sacrifice of the wise Raghunātha proceeded, / accompanied by sacrificial gifts, filled with excellent twice-born men, performing all auspicious rites.
Then Rāma’s younger brother went and bowed low to his mother: / "Grant permission; I am going to protect the horse, O auspicious lady!"
Having conquered the host of enemies by your grace, endowed with splendour, / I will return along with the great kings and the excellent horse.’
The mother said: / "Go, my son, great hero; may your paths be auspicious! / Having conquered all hosts of enemies, return, O virtuous one!
Protect Puṣkala, your brother’s son, most knowledgable in dharma; / though very strong, he is still a boy, fond of play.
O son, if you return accompanied by Puṣkala and endowed with fortune, / then there will be joy for me; otherwise I will share in grief.’
He replied to his mother who was thus conversing with him: / "Remembering your pair of feet, I shall attain good fortune."
Protecting Puṣkala like my own limb, O fair one, / and acting in a manner worthy of my name, I shall return rejoicing.’
Having spoken thus, the hero went to Rāma, who was seated in the sacrificial pavilion / with the foremost of excellent sages, wearing the splendid attire for sacrifice.
Endowed with all splendour, the wise hero said: / ‘O Rāma, command me for the sake of guarding the horse, by your permission.’
Raghunātha too, hearing that, said: ‘May it be auspicious! / You must not kill a child, a woman, an intoxicated person, or one without weapons.’
Then Lakṣmīnidhi, Janaka's son and brother to Jānakī, / smiling slightly and rolling his eyes, said to Rāma:
Lakṣmīnidhi said: / "O Rāmacandra, mighty-armed one, devoted to all dharma, / instruct Śatrughna so that he may be extraordinary.
Performing the duty befitting his lineage and acting as his elder brother did, / he will attain the supreme abode, endowed with splendor and might.
You have said, O great king: “One should not disrespect a brāhmaṇa.” / Yet a brāhmaṇa devoted to filial piety was slain by your father.’
You too performed a very great deed censured by the world, / since you surely killed a woman, one who should not be killed.
His elder brother, O great king, performed a feat of valor / which had been done by no one before: the cutting off of the ears of a rākṣasa woman.
Thus the king Śatrughna will act upon your instruction; / if he does not act so, it would be unworthy of his lineage."
To him who had spoken thus, Rāma, skilled in all manner of speech, / replied, smiling as it were, in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
"Let tranquil yogins, who look upon joy and sorrow as equal, listen: / they know how to cross over the shoreless ocean of worldly existence.
Those who are heroes with great bows, experts in all weapons and missiles, / they know about the matter of battle, but people like you do not.
Those who oppress others and those who stray onto evil paths / are to be slain by all kings who desire the welfare of all people."
Hearing what had been said, all those members of the assembly smiled at that subduer of enemies; / the pot-born [sage] released that very horse, which had been honored and was exceedingly adorned.
Uttering this mantra, Vasiṣṭha, [and] the pot-born [Agastya], / touching the horse with their fingertips, released it, desiring victory:
"O steed, go at your pleasure everywhere on the surface of the earth! / He for whose sacrifice you were released—return to him quickly!"
The horse, being released and surrounded by all the soldiers skilled in weapons and missiles, / set out toward the eastern quarter with the speed of the wind.
The whole army marched forth, causing the surface of the earth to tremble; / even Śeṣa supported the earth with a hood slightly bent.
The quarters became clear, the earth all around was filled with beauty, / and gentle breezes blew from behind Śatrughna.
As Śatrughna set out to depart, his right arm throbbed, / portending good fortune and indicating victory.
Puṣkala entered his delightful, prosperous house, / adorned with white verandas and jewel platforms.
There he saw his wife, devoted to her husband, / slightly thrilled at seeing him, yet longing to behold her lord.
With her lotus-like mouth she was chewing a betel leaf accompanied by fine camphor; / on her nose was a costly pearl born of the water, and beautiful bracelets on her lotus-stalk-like arms.

Her excellent breasts resembled wood-apple fruits, the curve of her hips was adorned with an excellent girdle, / and her feet, wearing anklets, were very delicate; bearing these, she looked upon her noble husband.
The resolute hero embraced his beloved, whose voice faltered [with emotion], / her body pressed tight against his chest in their embrace,
and said: "Auspicious lady, I am going as Śatrughna's rear guard, / in a chariot, protecting the sacrificial horse by Rāma’s command.
You must worship my mothers with massaging of their feet and the like, / eating their leftover food, zealously performing service for them.
All virtuous women devoted to their husbands, such as Lopāmudrā, / who are radiant with the power of their ascetic heat, must not be slighted by you, O timid one."

5.12.m: Śeṣa said: / Having looked with intense love upon her husband who had spoken thus, / she replied, smiling as it were, her voice faltering slightly:
"My lord, may you have victory everywhere on the circle of battle! / You must carry out Śatrughna's command so that the horse may be protected.
For I, your handmaid, following in your footsteps, should always be remembered; / my mind, my lord, never turns anywhere away from you.
Yet in the midst of battle, my beloved, never should I be remembered; / while I am present in your heart, victory in war would be in doubt.
O lotus-eyed one, act in such a way that Urmilā and the others / do not laugh at me, clapping their hands when they see me [and saying]:
'This is the wife of an utter coward, one who flees from the battlefield! / When even timid men fight, where is the time for heroes?'
"Act in such a way, O mighty-armed one, in guarding Rāma's horse, / that the celestial maidens do not laugh loudly at me."
Be the foremost fighter everywhere, with the others behind you; / let the mighty foes be deafened by the twang of your bow!
From dread of the sword held in your rising lotus-hand, / may the enemy's host be swiftly confounded by mutual panic!
Adorn your illustrious family by conquering your foes; / go, my lord, O mighty-armed one, may good fortune attend you here!
Take this bow at once, adorned with an excellent bowstring, / hearing whose roar the host of enemies is struck with terror.
Let these two quivers, filled with millions of arrows to crush millions of foes, / be strapped on for your welfare, O hero!
Don this stout armor on your body, lovely as Kāma, / which dispels the dense darkness with its great lightning-like brilliance.

Place this handsome, charming helmet upon your head, / along with these bright crest-ornaments adorned with jewels and gems."

Looking upon the hero's daughter whose speech was pure, / gazing upon her body with his lotus eyes,
The son of Bharata, conqueror of enemies, capable of waging battle, / attained supreme joy and, deeply composed, spoke to her:
Puṣkala said: / "O beloved, as you speak to me, so I shall do everything; / may your desired fame as the wife of a hero be splendid, O Kāntimatī!"
The valiant one took the armor, the splendid crown, / the bow, the two great quivers, and the sword, all given by Kāntimatī.
Putting all that on, endowed with great splendor, / the great warrior, skilled in all arms and missiles, shone exceedingly.
Him, rich in the splendor of weapons and missiles, adorned with a garland of heroes, / anointed with saffron, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and the like,
and adorned down to his knees with garlands of various flowers, / the virtuous Kāntimatī repeatedly honored there with a wave-offering of lights.
Having waved the lights over him many times and showered him repeatedly with pearls, / she embraced her husband, her eyes trembling with flowing tears.
Embracing her firmly, he comforted her for a long time: / "O wife of a hero, O Kāntimatī, do not despair over separation from me!
I shall return to your presence, O passionate lady devoted to your husband!" / Having thus addressed his wife, he mounted his splendid chariot.
Watching that excellent husband of hers depart, / she, devoted to her husband, looked on with unwinking eyes.
He went to see his father and his mother who was frantic with love; / having approached his father and mother, he joyfully bowed his head to them.
Embracing her son, the mother seated him on her lap; / shedding a stream of tears, she said: "May you be safe!"
He said to his father Bharata: "Rāma is performing the supreme sacrifice; / he must be protected by Lakṣmaṇa and by you great-souled ones."
Commanded by his mother and by his father with joyful words, / he set out for Śatrughna's camp, which was adorned with mighty heroes.
Surrounded by chariot-warriors, foot-soldiers, heroes, fine steeds, and horsemen, / the leader in front of the great sacrificial horse of the crest-jewel of the Raghus went forth with joy.
Marching through the Pāñcāla lands, the Kurus, and the Northern Kurus, / and through Daśārṇa and the magnificent territories, endowed with all glory,
hearing everywhere all the glory of the hero of the Raghus / who protected his devotees by slaying the rākṣasa Rāvaṇa,
and how Rāma, having undertaken the sacred task of the horse sacrifice, / spreading his fame throughout the world, protected the people from fear,
the great and eminent Śatrughna, pleased with them, / bestowed necklaces, various gems, and very costly garments.
The minister of the lord of the Raghus named Sumati, brilliant, / skilled in all sciences, was an excellent follower of Śatrughna.
Accompanied by him, the mighty hero passed through many villages and countrysides; / by the majesty of the lord of the Raghus, no one seized the horse.
Many rulers of lands, possessed of great strength and prowess, / endowed with fourfold armies of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers,
bringing abundant riches together with pearls and rubies, / bowed repeatedly before Śatrughna, who had arrived to protect the horse, [saying]:
"This entire kingdom and wealth, along with sons, livestock, and kinsmen, / belongs entirely to Rāmacandra, O descendant of Raghu, not to me!"
Hearing what they said, Śatrughna, slayer of enemy heroes, / made known his command there and proceeded along the path together with them.
Thus, in due course, accompanied by the horse, Śatrughna / reached the city of Ahicchatrā, O sage, teeming with various peoples,
crowded with brāhmaṇas, adorned with various jewels, / and embellished with mansions and gate-towers of gold and crystal,
where lotus-faced women who surpassed Rambhā / were seen in all the palaces, full of graceful charm,
where the people, refined in conduct and enjoying every pleasure, / were full of playful grace like the attendants of Kubera,
and where bow-wielding heroes skilled in aiming arrows / kept their king, named Sumada, exceedingly delighted.
From afar the lord beheld such a city; / on its outskirts lay an excellent garden filled with beauty,
with punnāgas, nāgacampakas, tilakas, devadārus, / aśokas, pāṭalas, mangos, mandāras, kovidāras,
sweet mangos, jambus, kadambas, priyālas, and jackfruits, / śālas, palmyras, tamālas, mallikās, jātis, yūthikās,
nīpas, kadambas, bakulas, campakas, madanas, and the like; / then Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, saw that garden adorned with them.
and right behind it marched the hero, / whose lotus-like feet were served by bowmen.
There he beheld a marvelous temple of the deity / adorned with sapphires, cat's-eye gems, and emeralds,
worthy of being served by the gods, resembling a peak of Kailāsa, / the best of abodes, adorned with pillars of gold.
Seeing that excellent temple of the deity, the brother of the lord of the Raghus / questioned his minister Sumati, the best of speakers:
Śatrughna said: / "Tell me, best of ministers: What is this? Whose divine temple is this? / What deity is worshipped here? For what reason does it stand here, O sinless one?"
Hearing this, the all-knowing [minister], conversant with counsel, replied: / "Listen with a single mind, O hero, to everything here as it is:
Know this to be the supreme shrine of Kāmākṣā, bestower of sole peace upon the universe, / by the mere sight of whom all perfection is attained, O lord of men!
By praising and bowing to her, gods and demons have obtained all fortune; / she is the compassionate granter of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation to her devotees."
Implored formerly by Sumada, the ruler of Ahicchatrā, / she stays here, fulfilling all desires and taking away the sorrow of her devotees.
Bow to her, Śatrughna, crest-jewel of all heroes! / Having bowed down, you will quickly attain perfection difficult even for gods and asuras to reach.
Hearing those words, Śatrughna, the scorcher of his foes, / that bull among men, asked for all the news of Bhavānī.
Śatrughna said: / Who was the king Sumada, the ruler of Ahicchatrā? What austerity did he perform, / by which this mother of all the worlds, pleased, remained established here?
Tell everything, great minister, enriched with varied significance; / since you know it correctly, speak, O highly intelligent one!
Sumati said: / There is the holy mountain Hemakūṭa, adorned by all the gods; / there is a pure sacred bath, well served by multitudes of sages.
Sumada, indeed, whose mother, father, and subjects were slain / by enemies along with all his feudatories, went there to perform austerity.
For three years, standing on one foot, remembering with focused mind, / he meditated on the mother of the worlds, his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose.
For three years, sustaining himself by eating dry leaves, / he performed most severe and exceedingly difficult austerity.
For three years he plunged into water during the cold season, / observed the five fires in summer, and faced the rain clouds during the rains.
Restraining his breath within his mind for three years, / the steadfast man, remembering Bhavānī, saw nothing around him.
When the twelfth year had passed, seeing this supreme austerity / and pondering it deeply in his mind, Śakra rivalled him out of fear.
He commanded Kāma, surrounded by his retinue, / accompanied by apsarases, and set upon conquering Brahmā, Indra, and others:
Go, Kāma, my friend, and do me a service, O bewildering one! / Act so that an obstacle may arise to the austerity of Sumada.
Hearing that momentous speech, the mighty Turāsāha himself, / full of ripe pride in conquering the universe, spoke, O descendant of Raghu:
Kāma said: / Master, who is this Sumada, and what is his trifling austerity? / I break the austerities of Brahmā and others; what then to speak of him?
Pierced by the power of my arrows, the Moon approached Tārā in the past; / you too approached Ahalyā, and Viśvāmitra approached Menakā.
Do not worry, lord of the gods, while I, your servant, am here. / Here I go against Sumada; protect the gods, venerable one!
Having spoken thus, the love-god went to the Hemakūṭa mountain, / accompanied by his friend Spring, as well as by troops of apsarases.
Spring immediately endowed all the trees there with flowers and fruits, / and made cuckoos resound alongside rows of bees.
A very cool breeze blew, originating from the southern quarter, / carrying clove flowers from the banks of the Kṛtamālā river.
In the forest thus transformed, the best of apsarases named Rambhā, / accompanied by her female friends, went near Sumada.

There she began to sing, possessing a voice as charming as a Kinnara's, / skilled in various kinds of instruments such as mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas.

Hearing that singing, that ruler of men, / and beholding the enchanting spring,
as well as the delightful calling of the cuckoo, / the wise man turned his eyes.

Seeing that king awakened, Kāma, armed with flowers, hastening, / quickly strung his bow behind him, O sinless one.

One apsaras there [massaged] the king's feet, / her sprout-like eyes dancing as she massaged,
another discharged sidelong glances, / and yet another made intense movements of her limbs.
Surrounded in this way by apsarases, his mind agitated by desire, / the wise man, the crest-jewel of those who have conquered their senses, reflected:
These foremost apsarases, causes of obstacles to my austerity, / sent by Śakra, will do whatever they can.
Thinking thus, the man of severe penance spoke to those lovely women: / "Who are you? Where do you dwell? What do you wish to do?"
It is most wonderful indeed that you have come within range of my eyes! / You who are exceedingly difficult to attain by austerities have come to my austerity!

5.13.m: Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech of Sumada, the treasury of austerity, / the apsarases, the army of Kāma, headed by Rambhā, joyfully said to him:
Through your austerities, O beloved, all of us excellent women have been won; / enjoy the full wealth of their youth, abandon the fruit of austerity!

Let this fortunate Ghṛtācī, bearing a body radiant like a campaka flower, / taste the nectar of your mouth, charming with the fragrance of camphor.

"This woman, O fortunate one, possesses splendid grace, / enchanting limbs, and firm, plump, beautiful breasts;

enjoy her quickly, O beloved, obtained through your own severe merits; / and moreover, cast away all grief!

me also, adorned with priceless ornaments, / my chest resplendent with garlands of mandāra flowers,

expert in the discourse of various arts of love, / embrace firmly so that you hold [me] close!

drink the nectar flowing from my mouth, / having mounted the excellent celestial chariot with me.

and having reached the peak of Sumeru frequented by many meritorious souls, / enjoy the true fruit of your austerity!

Let Tilottamā, radiant with youth and beauty, / hold a sunshade over your head.

and two fine fly-whisks marked by an unbroken stream, / like the currents of the Gaṅgā, O best of handsome men!

Listen, sir, to the enchanting talk of love; / drink the nectar craved even by the hosts of gods."

having entered the garden named Nandana, / sport with these excellent women, O lord!

Hearing what was said, the wise king / pondered: "From where indeed have they arrived?
Were these celestial women created by me through penance, / or is this an obstacle? What must be done here?"
Distressed with thought in this way, reflecting in his mind, the wise, / intelligent, and heroic Sumada spoke to the heavenly women.
"Indeed, you abide in my heart, having the essential nature of the Mother of the Universe. / Whatever is meditated upon by me is also considered to have your form.
This heavenly pleasure described by you is trivial and accompanied by doubt; / my Sovereign Mistress, served by me with devotion, will grant my wish.
By whose grace Brahmā attained Satyaloka and became great, / she indeed, who puts an end to her devotees' suffering, will give me everything.
What is the Nandana garden, or what is the mountain adorned with gold? / What is the nectar, obtained through petty merit, that causes grief to the Dānavas?"
Hearing this speech, Kāma, with diverse arrows, / struck the lord of men, but was not able to achieve anything.
With sidelong glances, the tinkling of anklets, embraces, and amorous looks, / the excellent women were unable to make his mind wander.
Returning the way they had come, they said to Indra: "The king is resolute-minded." / Hearing that, Indra became afraid and began to serve him himself.
Then, seeing that he was resolute at her own lotus feet, / Ambikā became visible to the senses of the sense-restrained great king, being deeply pleased.
Graceful upon the back of a lion, holding a noose and a goad, the supreme goddess, / the Mother, bearer of bow and arrow, the purifier of that which purifies the universe—
beholding that Mother, possessed of a splendor equal to ten million suns, / holding a bow, arrow, goad, and nooses, the wise man was filled with joy.
Bowing repeatedly with his head to the Mother imbued with devotion, / smiling and repeatedly touching her on his limbs with his hand,
the great-minded one praised her, his mental movements stirred by devotion, / endowed with a choked voice, his body adorned with bristling hair:
"Victory, O Goddess! O Great Goddess, uniquely served by the host of devotees! / O sinless one, whose pair of feet is served by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra!
O Mother, all this animate and inanimate world shines forth, penetrated by a portion of you; / without you none of this exists; therefore, O auspicious Mother, salutations unto you!
The earth is maintained by you through your supporting power, and does not move here, / adorned with mountains, forests, parks, and elephants of the quarters.
The sun burns in the sky, scorching the earth with his sharp rays; / by your power he absorbs the sap dwelling on the earth and releases it.
May the fire situated inside and outside bring welfare to the worlds, / on account of your majesty, O Great Goddess bowed to by gods and asuras!
You are wisdom; you are the great illusion of Viṣṇu, the sole protector of the universe; / by your own power you create this, and you also protect it, O enchantress!
Having obtained power from you, all the gods indeed enjoy happiness. / Protect me, O mistress of compassion, O praised one, O beloved of devotees!
Protect me, your servant, O Mother, whose refuge is your feet; / fulfill my desired attainment, O elder born before the Supreme Spirit!"
Sumati said: / Thus pleased, the Mother of the Universe said to the devotee Sumada, / whose body had grown lean from austerities: "Choose an excellent boon."
Hearing this speech, King Sumada, overjoyed, / chose his own captured kingdom, freed of the thorns of wicked enemies,
unswerving devotion to the two feet of the Great Goddess, / and, at the end, liberation that carries one across the ocean of worldly existence.
Kāmākṣā said: / "Attain your kingdom, O Sumada, with its thorns destroyed on all sides; / become one whose lotus-like feet are attended by the jewels of women!
May there be no defeat from enemies for you, O one named Sumada! / When the highly renowned Raghunātha, having slain Rāvaṇa,
shall perform the horse sacrifice, adorned with all provisions, / his brother, the great hero Śatrughna, slayer of enemy heroes,
protecting the horse, will come here surrounded by warriors and others; / having surrendered everything—your flourishing kingdom, wealth, and the rest—to him,
you shall guard [it] along with your own fierce archer warriors; / then you will wander everywhere upon the earth, O wise one!
Then, having bowed to Rāma, who is served by Brahmā, Indra, Śiva, and the others, / you will attain liberation, which is hard to attain even for yogins through the disciplines of restraint.
I shall remain here for so long as the arrival of Rāma's horse; / afterwards, having uplifted you, I will go to the supreme abode."
Having spoken thus, the Goddess, revered by gods and asuras, vanished; / and Sumada, having slain his enemies in Ahicchatrā, became king.
Even though capable and possessed of forces and mounts, this king, well instructed by Mahāmāyā, will not seize your steed.
Hearing that the supreme horse of the horse sacrifice has arrived near his city, and that your feet are served by all great kings, O wise one,
The all-knowing king named Sumada will surrender everything now, O great king, by the majestic power of Rāmacandra.
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this account of Sumada, the glorious, / Wise, and powerful one said, “Well done! Well done!” and rejoiced.
Surrounded by all his retinue, the lord of Ahicchatrā / Sat comfortably in the assembly hall, attended by many kings.
Brāhmaṇas learned in the Vedas and Vaiśyas prosperous in wealth / Waited upon King Sumada, who was endowed with splendor.
Excellent righteous brāhmaṇas, taking delight in the lore of the Vedas, / Pronounced blessings upon that king, the sole protector of all the worlds.
At that time, someone came and said to the king: / “O master, I do not know whose horse it is that carries a letter nearby.”
Hearing that, he quickly dispatched his foremost servant: / “Find out to which king belongs this horse near my city.”
Then the servant went there, learned the whole story from the beginning, / And reported it to the king, who was served by great royalty.
Hearing it, and constantly remembering the horse of the lord of the Raghus, / The skilled king gave orders to all his people:
“All my people, filled with wealth and grain, / Let them set up auspicious arches and decorations on their houses here.
Let thousands of lovely maidens, adorned with all ornaments / And mounted on elephants, go out to meet Śatrughna.”
Having issued all such commands, the king himself then set forth, / surrounded by his retinue of sons, grandsons, queens, and others.
Śatrughna, accompanied by great ministers and excellent warriors like Puṣkala, / Saw the heroic king named Sumada,
Surrounded by elephants with their riders, foot-soldiers that scorch foes, / Adorned steeds, and heroic men, looking splendid in his valor.
Then, coming forward, the great king bowed to Śatrughna with joy: / “Blessed am I, my purpose is fulfilled, and my body has been made pure.
Quickly accept this kingdom, adorned by great kings, / Filled with great jewels, pearls, and immense riches.
O lord, for a long time I have awaited the arrival of the horse; / What was told earlier by Kāmākṣā has now come to pass just so.
Gaze upon my city, make its people fulfilled in their purpose, / And purify my entire family, O earth-lord, younger brother of Rāma!”
Having spoken thus, he had the great hero Puṣkala mount the elephant / splendid as the moon, and then he mounted it himself.
Then the sound of kettledrums, paṇavas, tūryas, lutes, and other instruments / Spread abroad, O great king, urged on by Sumada.

The maidens, coming up to the great sovereign Śatrughna whose feet are served by Indra and the gods, / Sent by the king, showered congratulations upon him from atop the elephants with heaps of pearls.
Advancing slowly into the midst of the city, / Congratulated joyfully by the people, he reached the palace decorated with triumphal arches and other ornaments.
Accompanied by the jewel of a horse and looking resplendent with heroes, / Honored by the king, King Śatrughna entered the palace.
Worshiping the younger brother of the lord of the Raghus with arghya and other offerings, / He surrendered everything to the wise Rāmacandra.
